children: ALPA India has offered support to the pilots, who reportedly want outstanding salaries cleared amid concerns over delayed payments and vendor services

Around 40 pilots operating SpiceJet’s Q400 aircraft have reportedly refused to fly until their pending salary dues are cleared, according to sources. The Airline Pilots’ Association of India (ALPA India) has expressed solidarity with the pilots and offered support in seeking a resolution.

The development comes as the budget carrier continues to face financial and operational challenges. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), the country’s aviation regulator, has been closely monitoring the airline.

Sources said on Monday that the pilots had recently refused to operate flights until their outstanding salaries were paid. Further details about the dues and the duration of the protest were not immediately available. SpiceJet did not comment on the matter.

In a letter dated 9 October addressed to its members and the civil aviation fraternity, ALPA India said it stood firmly in solidarity with the pilots. The association also offered moral support, along with logistical, professional and consultative assistance, to help pursue what it described as a fair and constructive resolution.
The association said it had been informed that a group of pilots operating SpiceJet’s Q400 fleet had taken a stand in defence of their rights, professional dignity and aviation safety standards.
According to ALPA India, the pilots had reportedly been working under considerable stress and uncertainty amid persistent financial and operational challenges at the airline.

The letter also referred to reports of unpaid vendors declining to provide essential aircraft-related services, alongside delayed salaries and outstanding employee benefits. ALPA India said these issues had contributed to an increasingly difficult working environment.

SpiceJet’s operational position remains under pressure. According to information available on aircraft fleet-tracking website Planespotters.net, the airline had an operational fleet of 10 aircraft, including two Q400s, while 37 aircraft were parked.
The reported refusal by the pilots to fly adds to the challenges facing the carrier as it works through its financial and operational difficulties.
The latest development also highlights concerns around salary payments and employee benefits, although the airline has not publicly commented on the reported dispute.
Further details regarding the outstanding dues, the number of affected flights and any discussions between the pilots and the airline were not immediately available.
